result:
The construction is greedy: choose each term to avoid a small interval around every earlier term.

**Construction.** Let $\zeta(a)=\sum_{d\ge1} d^{-a}$, which is finite since $a>1$. Set $C = 2\zeta(a)+1$. Define $x_0 = 0$, and for $n \ge 1$, having chosen $x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}$ in $[0,C]$, choose $x_n \in [0,C]$ outside every open interval
$$I_j = \bigl(x_j - (n-j)^{-a},\; x_j + (n-j)^{-a}\bigr), \qquad 0 \le j < n.$$

**Why $x_n$ exists.** The total length of the removed intervals is at most
$$\sum_{j<n} 2(n-j)^{-a} = 2\sum_{d=1}^{n} d^{-a} \le 2\zeta(a) < C.$$
A closed interval of length $C$ cannot be covered by open intervals of total length less than $C$, so some $x_n \in [0,C]$ lies outside all of them.

**Why the condition holds.** For $j<n$, $x_n \notin I_j$ means $|x_n - x_j| \ge (n-j)^{-a}$, i.e. $|x_n-x_j|\,|n-j|^a \ge 1$. Since the condition is symmetric in $i$ and $j$, it holds for every pair of distinct nonnegative integers.

So the sequence is bounded by $C = 2\zeta(a)+1$ and satisfies $|x_i-x_j|\,|i-j|^a \ge 1$ for all distinct $i,j$.

ANSWER: Greedy choice: $x_0=0$, and $x_n\in[0,\,2\zeta(a)+1]$ chosen outside all open intervals $(x_j-(n-j)^{-a},\,x_j+(n-j)^{-a})$ for $j<n$, where $\zeta(a)=\sum_{d\ge1}d^{-a}$. This sequence is bounded by $C=2\zeta(a)+1$ and satisfies $|x_i-x_j|\,|i-j|^a\ge 1$.
